qs.q: A coronary artery autopsy specimen from a patient who suffered a sudden fatal myocardial infarction demonstrates a ruptured fibrous cap with overlying luminal thrombosis. Which primary cellular component within the atherosclerotic plaque is responsible for weakening this cap via matrix metalloproteinase secretion?
o: Recruited T lymphocytes driving cell-mediated cytotoxicity against myocytes
Proliferating smooth muscle cells synthesizing protective collagen fibers
Endothelial progenitor cells attempting to repair damaged luminal surfaces
Resident mast cells releasing histamine and promoting localized edema
Activated macrophages consuming oxidized lipoproteins and releasing enzymes
qs.e: Plaque rupture is mediated by macrophages in the fibrous cap secreting matrix metalloproteinases that degrade collagen.

qs.q: Which microscopic and structural features are most characteristic of an atherosclerotic plaque that is considered 'vulnerable' to rupture and subsequent acute coronary syndrome?
o: Absence of inflammatory macrophages
High density of smooth muscle cells
Large lipid core and thin fibrous cap
Thick fibrous cap and small lipid core
qs.e: Vulnerable plaques possess a large atheromatous lipid core, a thin fibrous cap, and a high macrophage load, making them prone to rupture. Thick fibrous caps and a high density of smooth muscle cells actually provide stability to the plaque.

qs.q: What is the immediate pathophysiological consequence following the rupture of a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque that triggers acute coronary syndromes?
o: Massive proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells
Permanent normalization of systemic blood pressure
Immediate regression of the vascular lumen narrowing
Thrombosis due to exposure of the thrombogenic core
qs.e: Plaque disruption exposes a thrombogenic core, which leads to thrombosis and acute vessel occlusion underlying acute coronary syndromes. Vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation is a feature of chronic atherosclerosis rather than an immediate result of plaque rupture.

qs.q: What primary feature characterizes a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque prone to rupture?
o: Extensive collagen forming a dense scar
A complete absence of immune cells
A thick calcified cap with minimal lipids
A thin fibrous cap and high lipid content
qs.e: Vulnerable plaques have thin fibrous caps and high lipid content, making them susceptible to degradation by enzymes released by macrophages and T cells. Plaques with thick, calcified caps are typically more stable.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic morphological feature of a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque prone to rupture?
o: Thick fibrous cap with dense collagen
Small atheromatous core with calcifications
Absence of inflammation and smooth muscle
Thin fibrous cap and high macrophage load
qs.e: A vulnerable plaque features a large atheromatous core, a thin fibrous cap, fissures, and a high macrophage load that destabilizes the plaque. Stable plaques typically feature thicker fibrous caps.

qs.q: Which component of an atherosclerotic plaque directly overlies the necrotic core and consists primarily of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen?
o: Fibrous cap of plaque
Neovascular base region
Shoulder region of plaque
Fatty streak of intima
qs.e: The fibrous cap overlies the lipid-rich necrotic core and provides structural stability, consisting of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen. A vulnerable plaque has a thin cap, making it prone to rupture.

qs.q: Atherosclerotic plaque disruption leading to acute thrombosis most frequently occurs at which of the following locations?
o: Cortical bridging veins
Superior sagittal sinus
Basilar artery midpoint
Carotid bifurcation
qs.e: Thrombosis commonly arises from acute changes in vulnerable atherosclerotic plaques at the carotid bifurcation, origin of the middle cerebral artery, or either end of the basilar artery. The carotid bifurcation is a prime site for atheromatous plaques.

qs.q: A 67-year-old male smoker with diabetes presents with renovascular hypertension caused by an atherosclerotic plaque. At which specific anatomical location does this plaque typically form?
o: Distal interlobular branches
Origin of the renal artery
Juxtaglomerular arteriole wall
Arcuate vessel bifurcation
qs.e: Atherosclerotic plaques causing renal artery stenosis typically form right at the origin of the renal artery. Distal interlobular branches are more commonly affected by atheroembolism rather than origin plaque formation.

ai.title: Atherosclerotic Plaque
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque is a lipid‑laden, fibrous lesion that can rupture, causing thrombus and arterial occlusion. In low‑resource settings, infection, malnutrition and HIV accelerate plaque formation and instability.

sections.p: Atherosclerotic plaque is an intimal deposit of lipids, smooth‑muscle cells and connective tissue. It is diagnosed by imaging (ultrasound, CT angiography) or post‑mortem histology. In the ward, a history of chest pain and a raised troponin suggest plaque rupture.

t.b: Elevated troponin indicates myocardial necrosis due to plaque rupture and thrombus
ST‑segment elevation or new Q waves suggest acute coronary occlusion
Regional wall motion abnormality shows area supplied by occluded artery

sections.p: Severity is graded by the extent of luminal narrowing and plaque vulnerability. The Gensini score or SYNTAX score are used in research; clinically we use the degree of stenosis and presence of symptoms.
The main drivers are dyslipidaemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes and chronic infections common in East Africa. HIV and TB can accelerate inflammation and plaque instability.
Patients may have stable angina, unstable angina or an acute myocardial infarction. In the brain, plaque rupture can cause stroke.
b: Chest pain at rest or exertion

sections.p: Use bedside tests that are available. When advanced imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical scoring and simple labs.

t.b: High CRP indicates systemic inflammation that may destabilise plaque
LDL >130 mg/dL is a risk factor for plaque formation
Hypertension >140/90 mmHg contributes to endothelial injury
HbA1c >7% indicates poor glycaemic control, a risk for atherosclerosis

sections.p: Rupture leads to thrombosis and occlusion, causing MI or stroke. Complications include heart failure, arrhythmia and sudden death.
Treat the underlying cause, give antiplatelets, statins and control risk factors. In emergencies, reperfusion therapy is essential.
Regular monitoring of lipids, blood pressure and glucose. Lifestyle changes and adherence to medication reduce progression.
Plaque rupture is often mistaken for plaque erosion or coronary spasm. Erosion lacks a necrotic core, while spasm is a transient vasoconstriction.
b: Plaque erosion – thrombus without necrotic core

sections.p: Low‑grade troponin can be normal in early MI; normal CRP does not exclude plaque instability. Ultrasound may miss small coronary plaques.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe chest pain with diaphoresis

faq.q: Why is aspirin the first drug given in suspected MI?
faq.a: It blocks platelet aggregation, preventing further thrombus growth.

faq.q: What is the role of statins in plaque stability?
faq.a: They lower LDL and have anti‑inflammatory effects that strengthen the fibrous cap.
Yes, chronic inflammation and some antiretrovirals raise lipid levels, accelerating plaque formation.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with crushing chest pain at rest. ECG shows ST elevation in V2‑V4. What is the first step in management? — Give aspirin, oxygen and prepare for reperfusion therapy.
A patient with known coronary artery disease has sudden dyspnoea and a new Q‑wave on ECG. What complication is most likely? — Myocardial infarction due to plaque rupture.
Why is a high‑dose beta‑blocker avoided in a patient with asthma? — It can trigger bronchospasm.
A patient with HIV on protease inhibitors has high LDL. What lipid‑lowering strategy is preferred? — Statin therapy, avoiding fibrates due to drug interactions.
What is the most common cause of plaque rupture in low‑resource settings? — Chronic infections such as TB or HIV causing systemic inflammation.
A 60‑year‑old woman with hypertension presents with sudden left‑sided weakness. CT shows no bleed. What is the likely diagnosis? — Ischaemic stroke from plaque rupture in a large artery.
